blocks.text: Named entity recognition, NER, is a specific and widely used token classification task, covered generally in the previous topic, that identifies and categorizes real-world entities mentioned in text, people, organizations, locations, dates, and similar categories.
This topic covers common entity categories, the specific challenges of ambiguous and nested entities, and how NER differs when applied to specialized domains rather than general text.
1. What NER Does

blocks.alt: A raw sentence goes through an NER model, producing tagged entities

blocks.text: NER applies the token classification approach covered in the previous topic to a specific goal, finding spans of text that refer to named entities and labeling what type of entity each one is, a foundational building block for many downstream information extraction applications.
2. Common Entity Categories

blocks.alt: PER for person, ORG for organization, LOC for location, and DATE for date are common categories

blocks.text: General purpose NER systems commonly recognize categories like PER for people, ORG for organizations, LOC for locations, and DATE for dates, though the exact category set is defined per project and can be extended with domain-specific entity types as needed.
3. NER in Practice

blocks.alt: A sentence about Satya Nadella and Microsoft in Redmond yields extracted PER, ORG, and LOC entities

blocks.text: Applied to a sentence like "Satya Nadella leads Microsoft in Redmond," an NER model identifies Satya Nadella as a person, Microsoft as an organization, and Redmond as a location, using the BIO tagging scheme covered in the previous topic under the hood to mark exactly where each entity span begins and ends.
4. General Domain vs Specialized Domain NER

blocks.alt: General domain NER covers people and places while specialized domain NER covers drug or gene names

blocks.text: Beyond the general categories, specialized domains define their own entity types entirely, biomedical NER identifies drug names or gene names, legal NER identifies case citations or statute references, a model fine-tuned on general domain data transfers poorly to these specialized categories without domain-specific training data.
5. Handling Ambiguous Entity Mentions

blocks.alt: Washington could be tagged as a person or a location depending on context

blocks.text: The same surface text can refer to different entity types depending on context, "Washington" could be a person, George Washington, or a location, Washington State, resolving this ambiguity correctly requires the model to use surrounding context, training data needs enough varied examples of ambiguous names used in different senses.

blocks.title: Context, not the word alone, resolves ambiguity
blocks.content: A model relying too heavily on memorized word-to-label associations rather than surrounding context will systematically mishandle ambiguous entity mentions, varied contextual training examples are the main defense against this.

blocks.text: 6. Nested and Overlapping Entities

blocks.alt: Bank of America Tower contains a nested organization name within a building name

blocks.text: Some entity mentions genuinely nest inside each other, "Bank of America Tower" is a building name that itself contains an organization name, standard flat BIO tagging, covered in the previous topic, cannot represent this nesting directly, specialized nested NER approaches exist for cases where this matters, though many practical systems simplify by choosing the most useful single level.
7. NER as a Foundation for Structured Extraction

blocks.alt: Extracted entities feed knowledge graph linking, producing a structured record

blocks.text: NER output commonly feeds further processing, linking an extracted entity to a specific record in a knowledge base, or populating a structured record from unstructured text, NER itself only identifies and categorizes entity mentions, this further linking and structuring is typically a separate downstream step.
8. Evaluating NER Models

Entity-level F1, covered generally in the previous Token Tasks topic, is the standard NER evaluation metric, requiring a full entity span to be correctly identified and correctly typed, a partial match, getting the span right but the type wrong, or vice versa, both count as errors under strict entity-level evaluation.
9. Common Production Use Cases

NER commonly powers resume parsing, contract analysis, news entity extraction for knowledge graphs, and redacting personally identifiable information from documents, cases where automatically pulling out structured entity mentions from free text saves substantial manual effort.
Worked Example

A legal technology team fine-tunes an NER model to extract case citations, party names, and statute references from legal documents, categories the general domain PER, ORG, LOC, DATE scheme does not cover well.

Initial entity-level F1 is disappointing, review reveals many errors involve nested entities, a party name embedded within a longer case citation string, prompting the team to redefine their annotation scheme to prioritize the citation-level span as the primary label, resolving most of the nested entity confusion and improving entity-level F1 substantially.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a general domain entity category set for a specialized domain that needs its own custom entity types
Underrepresenting ambiguous entity mentions in training data, leaving the model reliant on memorized word associations
Not deciding upfront how to handle nested entities, leading to inconsistent annotation and confused model behavior
Evaluating with token-level rather than entity-level metrics, masking boundary and typing errors

blocks.text: Practice

Take a short paragraph of text and manually annotate it with PER, ORG, LOC, and DATE entity tags using the BIO scheme, then identify any ambiguous mentions or nested entities you encounter and how you resolved them.
Key Takeaway

Named entity recognition identifies and categorizes real-world entity mentions in text using the token classification approach covered in the previous topic, with domain-specific entity types, ambiguous mentions, and nested entities all requiring deliberate handling in both annotation and evaluation, and entity-level F1 remaining the standard way to judge whether a model reliably gets full entity spans right.
